title: Reproductive Hormone Biochemistry
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows sex steroids from cholesterol to their active forms and out through the liver, then covers the glycoprotein hormones and the chemistry of semen. Each topic is built around one enzyme step, one shared structure, or one clearance route, so a single defect explains a whole clinical picture: ambiguous genitalia in 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, endometrial hyperplasia in obesity, hyperthyroidism in molar pregnancy, and feminization in cirrhosis. Board questions usually give the phenotype or the lab pattern and ask for the missing or overactive enzyme, so the goal is to read the pathway well enough to predict what accumulates and what goes missing.

connections.how: The enzymes in this chapter make the hormones whose secretion, transport on SHBG, and feedback RE-7 describes.
The gonads share StAR, side-chain cleavage, 3-beta-HSD, and CYP17 with the adrenal cortex, so several enzyme defects affect cortisol and sex steroids together.
Loss of hepatic steroid clearance and portosystemic shunting explain the endocrine signs of cirrhosis.

The enzyme that removes carbon 19 and aromatizes the A ring, converting androgens into estrogens.
The enzyme that reduces testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT); type 2 predominates in genital skin and prostate, type 1 in sebaceous skin and liver.

sections.title: From cholesterol to progesterone, androgens, and estrogens

blocks.text: Sex steroids are made on demand rather than stored, so secretion rate equals synthesis rate. Their substrate is cholesterol (27 carbons), taken up mainly from plasma LDL. Products are classified by carbon number: progestins have 21 carbons, androgens 19, and estrogens 18.

The rate-limiting step is transfer of cholesterol from the outer to the inner mitochondrial membrane by StAR, where CYP11A1 cleaves the side chain to form pregnenolone, the precursor of every steroid hormone. LH acts on Leydig and theca cells through Gs, cAMP, and protein kinase A, acutely increasing StAR activity and, over hours to days, transcription of CYP11A1 and later enzymes.

In the smooth endoplasmic reticulum, two enzymes decide the fate of pregnenolone. 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (3-beta-HSD) oxidizes the 3-hydroxyl group and moves the double bond from the B ring to the A ring (delta-5 to delta-4), making progesterone. CYP17 adds a hydroxyl at carbon 17 (17-alpha-hydroxylase), then cuts the bond between carbons 17 and 20 (17,20-lyase), leaving a 19-carbon androgen. Human 17,20-lyase prefers 17-hydroxypregnenolone, so the main gonadal route runs through dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), which 3-beta-HSD converts to androstenedione.

17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (17-beta-HSD) reduces the 17-keto group, making testosterone from androstenedione and estradiol from estrone. Aromatase removes carbon 19 and aromatizes the A ring, making estradiol from testosterone and estrone from androstenedione, so every estrogen passes through an androgen first.

blocks.caption: The enzyme set of each cell type determines its product.

blocks.text: Which enzymes a cell expresses decides what it secretes. Leydig cells secrete testosterone. In the follicle, theca cells have LH receptors and CYP17 but little aromatase, while avascular granulosa cells have FSH receptors and aromatase but no CYP17, so the two must cooperate. The vascularized corpus luteum takes up LDL cholesterol and makes large amounts of progesterone. The placenta lacks CYP17 and builds estrogens from fetal adrenal DHEA sulfate.

blocks.text: A block causes deficiency of everything downstream and diverts precursor into the branches still open. Defects in enzymes shared with the adrenal cortex also disturb cortisol and mineralocorticoids.

blocks.title: Working through CYP17 deficiency
blocks.text: A 16-year-old with female genitalia has primary amenorrhea, no breast development, hypertension, and hypokalemia. Without CYP17, pregnenolone can go only toward progesterone and the mineralocorticoid branch. Low cortisol raises ACTH, which drives production of 11-deoxycorticosterone, a mineralocorticoid that retains Na+ and wastes K+; volume expansion suppresses renin and aldosterone. No androgen means no estrogen, so puberty fails and LH and FSH are high. If the karyotype is 46,XY, no testosterone or DHT was made, but Sertoli cell AMH still removed the uterus.

Testosterone and dihydrotestosterone (DHT) act through the same intracellular androgen receptor, a nuclear receptor that binds androgen response elements on DNA. DHT binds the receptor with higher affinity and dissociates more slowly, so it gives a stronger, more sustained signal at the same concentration. DHT also cannot be aromatized, so its effects are purely androgenic. 5-alpha-reductase reduces the A ring double bond of testosterone to make DHT inside target cells.

Two isoenzymes matter. Type 2 predominates in genital skin, the prostate and urogenital sinus, and scalp and beard follicles; type 1 predominates in sebaceous glands, nongenital skin, and liver. In the male fetus, the Wolffian ducts lie beside the testis and respond to high local testosterone, forming the epididymis, vas deferens, and seminal vesicles. The genital tubercle, urogenital folds, labioscrotal swellings, and urogenital sinus are farther away and need DHT to form the penis, scrotum, and prostate.

5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency is autosomal recessive and shows only in 46,XY individuals. The testes are normal, so Sertoli cell AMH removes the Mullerian ducts and Leydig cell testosterone builds normal Wolffian structures. With little DHT the external genitalia are ambiguous or appear female at birth, with a small phallus, bifid scrotum, perineoscrotal hypospadias, and a blind vaginal pouch, and the testes lie in the inguinal canals or labioscrotal folds.

At puberty, testosterone rises to adult levels, high enough to act on the androgen receptor directly and helped by type 1 activity in skin. The phallus grows, muscle mass increases, the voice deepens, and the testes may descend. DHT-dependent features stay weak: the prostate remains small, facial and body hair is sparse, temporal hair recession and acne are absent. Breast development does not occur because testosterone and estradiol are in normal male proportion. Labs show normal or high testosterone, normal or mildly raised LH, low DHT, and a high testosterone to DHT ratio, which widens after hCG stimulation.

blocks.title: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency versus complete androgen insensitivity
rows: Breast development from aromatized testosterone; scant pubic and axillary hair
Normal or mildly raised LH; high testosterone to DHT ratio
High LH, high testosterone, high estradiol for a male
blocks.caption: Wolffian ducts show whether testosterone could act: present when only DHT is missing, absent when the receptor fails.

blocks.predict: An adult man takes a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor for several months. Which tissues change, and which do not?
blocks.explain: The prostate shrinks and serum PSA falls by about half, and scalp hair loss slows, because these depend on DHT. Libido, muscle mass, and spermatogenesis are largely preserved because they are testosterone actions, and testosterone rises slightly as less is converted.

sections.title: Peripheral aromatization, obesity, and unopposed estrogen

blocks.text: Aromatase is expressed outside the gonads, most importantly in adipose stromal cells (preadipocytes), and also in skin, bone, brain, and liver. Adipose aromatase converts circulating androstenedione, mainly from the adrenal cortex and, after menopause, the ovarian stroma, into estrone. Estrone is a weaker estrogen, but target tissues convert some of it to estradiol with 17-beta-HSD. Because the enzyme needs only a circulating precursor, estrone output scales with fat mass rather than ovarian function, and fractional conversion increases with age and obesity.

blocks.title: Main source of estrogen by physiological state
rows: Granulosa cells of the dominant follicle and corpus luteum
Aromatization of adrenal and ovarian stromal androstenedione in fat
Placenta, using fetal adrenal DHEA sulfate
Mostly peripheral aromatization of testosterone; a small share from the testis
blocks.caption: Outside the reproductive years in women, and in men, most estrogen is made peripherally.

blocks.text: In the cycling endometrium, estrogen drives glandular and stromal proliferation through estrogen receptor alpha. Progesterone from the corpus luteum opposes it: it reduces estrogen receptor expression, induces 17-beta-HSD type 2, which converts estradiol to the weaker estrone, converts the glands to a secretory state, and, when it falls at the end of the cycle, triggers orderly shedding. Peripheral estrone is continuous and is not paired with progesterone. In obesity, especially with anovulation as in polycystic ovary syndrome or after menopause, the endometrium proliferates without interruption.

blocks.title: Obesity to endometrial hyperplasia
steps: Excess adipose tissue increases total aromatase

No ovulation, so no luteal progesterone
Continuous estrogen-driven proliferation without shedding
Hyperplasia, then atypia and endometrioid carcinoma
blocks.caption: Progression to atypical hyperplasia and endometrioid carcinoma involves acquired mutations such as PTEN loss on this estrogen-driven background.

blocks.text: Clinically this appears as heavy or irregular bleeding, or postmenopausal bleeding, from a thickened unstable endometrium. Obesity is a major risk factor for endometrioid (type I) endometrial carcinoma, while serous (type II) carcinoma arises on an atrophic endometrium and is not estrogen driven. Peripheral estrogen also raises the risk of postmenopausal estrogen receptor positive breast cancer.

In men, adipose aromatase converts testosterone to estradiol. Estrogen stimulates ductal epithelium and periductal stroma in the breast, producing gynecomastia, which is true glandular tissue palpable beneath the areola, unlike the diffuse fat of pseudogynecomastia. Estradiol also exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, lowering LH and therefore testicular testosterone, while low SHBG from insulin resistance lowers total testosterone further.

sections.title: The glycoprotein hormones: shared alpha, specific beta

blocks.text: hCG, LH, FSH, and TSH are heterodimers of two noncovalently joined, glycosylated subunits. The alpha subunit is identical in all four and is encoded by one gene; each beta subunit is encoded separately and determines which receptor the hormone activates. Neither subunit is active alone, so the free subunits have no hormonal effect. All four receptors are G protein-coupled receptors that signal mainly through Gs and cAMP.

blocks.title: The four glycoprotein hormones
rows: LH/hCG receptor; Leydig, theca, luteal cells
Androgen synthesis; ovulation; corpus luteum function
FSH receptor; Sertoli and granulosa cells
Spermatogenesis support; aromatase induction; follicle growth
Thyroid hormone synthesis and release; thyroid growth
Rescues the corpus luteum to maintain progesterone in early pregnancy
blocks.caption: The beta subunit decides the receptor; hCG and LH share one receptor.

blocks.text: The hCG and LH beta subunits are highly similar, so hCG binds the LH receptor. Early in pregnancy this lets trophoblast hCG keep the corpus luteum secreting progesterone until the placenta takes over progesterone production at about 8 to 10 weeks. The hCG beta subunit also has a carboxy-terminal extension of about 24 amino acids carrying O-linked sugars rich in sialic acid, which slows clearance and gives hCG a half-life of roughly a day or more, compared with about 20 minutes for LH. Serum hCG roughly doubles every 2 days in early pregnancy and peaks at about 8 to 10 weeks.

Because the alpha subunit is shared, an assay for it cannot distinguish the hormones. Pregnancy tests and tumor marker assays therefore use antibodies against beta-hCG, usually including its unique carboxy-terminal region, so they do not cross-react with LH.

Receptor specificity is high but not absolute. hCG is a weak agonist at the TSH receptor, many thousands of times less potent than TSH, which matters only when hCG is very high. In normal pregnancy the first-trimester hCG peak raises free T4 slightly and lowers TSH, the mirror image of the hCG curve. In a hydatidiform mole, especially a complete mole, or a choriocarcinoma, the abnormal trophoblast secretes far more hCG, and the result can be overt hyperthyroidism. The same excess drives the LH receptor on ovarian theca cells, producing bilateral theca lutein cysts, and hCG-secreting testicular germ cell tumors stimulate Leydig cell aromatase, causing gynecomastia.

blocks.caption: The thyroid is driven from outside the pituitary axis, so TSH is suppressed while thyroid hormone is high, and the hyperthyroidism resolves as hCG falls.

blocks.predict: A healthy woman at 10 weeks of gestation has a TSH slightly below the nonpregnant reference range. Is her pituitary failing?
blocks.explain: No. hCG peaks near 10 weeks and weakly stimulates the TSH receptor, raising thyroid hormone a little and suppressing TSH by normal feedback. As hCG falls in the second trimester, TSH returns toward normal.

sections.title: Hepatic inactivation of sex steroids and the feminization of cirrhosis

blocks.text: Steroids are lipid soluble and would be reabsorbed by the kidney if excreted unchanged, so the liver makes them water soluble in two phases. Phase I reactions, largely cytochrome P450 hydroxylations and 17-beta-HSD oxidation, reduce activity: estradiol is oxidized to estrone and hydroxylated to catechol estrogens, and testosterone is oxidized at carbon 17 and reduced in the A ring to androsterone and etiocholanolone. Phase II reactions then attach glucuronic acid (UDP-glucuronosyltransferases) or sulfate (sulfotransferases). The conjugates are excreted in urine, where androgen metabolites appear as 17-ketosteroids, or in bile.

Biliary estrogen conjugates can be deconjugated by bacterial beta-glucuronidase in the gut and reabsorbed, an enterohepatic circulation that returns part of the estrogen to the blood. Conjugates leave hepatocytes into bile or into plasma for renal excretion, so urinary metabolites reflect total production. Because the liver also makes SHBG, it controls both how much steroid is cleared and how much circulates free.

Cirrhosis shifts the balance toward estrogen through several mechanisms acting together. Reduced hepatocyte mass lowers estrogen inactivation. Portosystemic shunting carries adrenal androstenedione past the liver to adipose tissue and skin, where it is aromatized to estrone. SHBG usually rises, and because SHBG binds testosterone more tightly than estradiol, free testosterone falls more than free estradiol. In alcoholic cirrhosis, ethanol is also directly toxic to Leydig cells and suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. The net result is a high ratio of free estrogen to free androgen.

sections.title: Chemistry of semen and the meaning of PSA

blocks.text: Semen is mostly accessory gland fluid; sperm from the testes and epididymis contribute only about 5% of its volume. Normal ejaculate volume is about 1.5 to 5 mL with a pH of about 7.2 to 8.0, which buffers the acidic vagina. Each gland adds its own chemical marker, so semen chemistry can localize a problem in the male tract.

blocks.title: Contributions to semen
rows: Fructose (sperm energy), prostaglandins, semenogelin (forms the coagulum)
PSA (liquefies the coagulum), citrate, zinc, acid phosphatase
Mucus that lubricates the urethra and neutralizes residual acidic urine before ejaculation
blocks.caption: Fructose marks seminal vesicle fluid; PSA, citrate, and zinc mark prostatic fluid.

blocks.text: Seminal vesicle fluid enters through the ejaculatory ducts and supplies fructose, which sperm use for glycolysis. Semenogelin forms a gel coagulum immediately after ejaculation that holds the sperm. PSA, a kallikrein-family serine protease secreted by prostatic luminal epithelium under androgen control, cleaves semenogelin and liquefies the coagulum within about 15 to 30 minutes, freeing motile sperm. Prostatic citrate chelates calcium and contributes to buffering, and zinc has antibacterial activity and stabilizes sperm chromatin.

PSA is secreted into the gland lumen, separated from blood by the epithelium, a basal cell layer, and a basement membrane. Only a small amount normally reaches serum, where most is bound to alpha-1-antichymotrypsin. Serum PSA rises whenever there is more prostate tissue or a breach of this barrier, so it is specific to the prostate but not to cancer. It rises in benign prostatic hyperplasia (more epithelium), acute prostatitis (inflammation disrupts the epithelium), prostatic infarction, after instrumentation, and in carcinoma, where the disorganized glands and absent basal layer let PSA leak directly into the stroma and capillaries. Because prostate growth is DHT dependent, reducing DHT lowers PSA, linking this section to C02.

blocks.title: Localizing obstruction from semen chemistry
blocks.text: A man has azoospermia, ejaculate volume of 0.8 mL, acidic pH, and absent fructose. Fructose comes only from the seminal vesicles, so its absence means their fluid is missing. Without that alkaline majority, the low volume is mostly acidic prostatic fluid, which explains the pH. Two lesions fit: obstruction of the ejaculatory ducts, or congenital absence of the vas deferens, often with absent or hypoplastic seminal vesicles, as seen with CFTR mutations. Compare a man with azoospermia but normal volume, pH, and fructose: the seminal vesicles and ejaculatory ducts are intact, so the problem lies in the testis or the epididymis and vas above the seminal vesicles.

integration.text: Biochemistry and embryology explain the developmental disorders. One cholesterol-derived pathway feeds the adrenal, testis, ovary, and placenta, and each tissue's enzyme set decides its output, so shared enzymes (StAR, CYP11A1, 3-beta-HSD, CYP17) cause combined adrenal and gonadal disease while peripheral enzymes (5-alpha-reductase, aromatase) cause isolated reproductive phenotypes. The Wolffian ducts, the external genitalia, and the prostate differ in which androgen they need, so the anatomy of a 46,XY infant reveals which step failed. The same logic applies to the glycoprotein hormones: one shared alpha subunit and similar beta subunits explain both normal corpus luteum rescue and the thyroid and ovarian effects of trophoblastic disease.

Physiology and pathology connect peripheral metabolism to disease. Adipose aromatase, hepatic clearance, and SHBG binding all change the ratio of free estrogen to free androgen without any change in the gonads, which is why obesity, cirrhosis, and menopause share features such as gynecomastia or endometrial hyperplasia. Total hormone levels can mislead when SHBG changes, and PSA reflects prostate tissue and barrier integrity rather than malignancy itself.

summary: StAR transfer of cholesterol into mitochondria is rate limiting; CYP11A1 makes pregnenolone, the precursor of every steroid, and LH stimulates both through cAMP.

3-beta-HSD makes progesterone and androstenedione, CYP17 converts 21-carbon steroids to 19-carbon androgens, 17-beta-HSD makes testosterone and estradiol, and aromatase makes estrogens from androgens.
Theca cells (LH, CYP17) make androstenedione and granulosa cells (FSH, aromatase) convert it to estradiol; the placenta lacks CYP17 and uses fetal DHEA sulfate.
DHT binds the androgen receptor more strongly than testosterone and is required for the external genitalia and prostate; Wolffian ducts need only testosterone.
5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency gives a 46,XY infant ambiguous genitalia with normal Wolffian ducts, virilization at puberty, and a high testosterone to DHT ratio.
Adipose aromatase turns androstenedione into estrone, the main postmenopausal estrogen; without progesterone this causes endometrial hyperplasia, and in men gynecomastia and low LH.
hCG, LH, FSH, and TSH share one alpha subunit; beta subunits give specificity, so assays measure beta-hCG and very high hCG can activate TSH and LH receptors.

The liver inactivates sex steroids and conjugates them to glucuronides and sulfates; cirrhosis raises the free estrogen to androgen ratio through reduced clearance, shunting to aromatase, and higher SHBG.
Seminal vesicles supply fructose and semenogelin; the prostate supplies PSA, citrate, and zinc, and PSA liquefies the coagulum.
Serum PSA rises with more prostate tissue or barrier disruption, so BPH, prostatitis, and carcinoma all raise it.

verify: The share of male estradiol made by peripheral aromatization (often quoted as about 80%) and the testicular share vary among sources; this chapter says only most versus a small share.

Semen volume and composition figures (seminal vesicles about 60 to 70%, prostate about 20 to 30%, volume about 1.5 to 5 mL, pH about 7.2 to 8.0) follow common references and WHO-based values; confirm the values NABNE uses.
The hCG half-life (quoted from about 24 to 36 hours) and the length of the beta-subunit carboxy-terminal extension (about 24 amino acids, sometimes 28 to 31) differ slightly among sources.
No hCG threshold for hyperthyroidism in molar pregnancy is given because published cutoffs vary; confirm whether NABNE expects a value.
The relative contribution of reduced estrogen clearance, peripheral aromatization, and raised SHBG to feminization in cirrhosis differs among sources; all three are presented as contributing.
Serum PSA reference limits (often below about 4 ng/mL, with age-specific ranges) are not stated here because cutoffs vary; confirm whether NABNE Part I tests a value.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the CYP gene names (CYP11A1, CYP17, CYP19) and isoenzyme numbers for 17-beta-HSD and 5-alpha-reductase, or only the enzyme names.
